narrative:
The model predicted a 66% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the third decile is noticeably lower than the average of sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling that your early performance was weaker than most successful applicants. Your third-year ranking followed closely behind, also pulling the outcome toward failure; again, a third-decile placement sits below the roughly sixth-decile average of admitted students.

Your LSAT score was the only major factor working in your favor. A score of 43 is substantially higher than the 37-point average among accepted students, which helped reduce the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the combined impact of your two class-rank indicators.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.0, middle-income background, and plan to attend full-time were less influential and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record in any remaining coursework, consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it further, or explore schools with different admissions thresholds. You may also want to gather letters of recommendation that highlight growth since your first year.
